comparison: Both strongly support the main findings (C2, C3) that TMEM127 loss causes RET accumulation and constitutive signaling. OpenEval evaluates the synthesis of experimental evidence, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm these as 'convincing evidence' with multiple reviewers praising the mechanistic insights.

Both support findings on RET protein accumulation (C41, C42, C47). OpenEval emphasizes the comprehensive experimental validation including rescue experiments, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the overall 'compelling cellular and biochemical evidence.'

Both support the constitutive signaling findings (C127-C129, C133). OpenEval highlights the use of multiple RET inhibitors strengthening causal links, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the mechanistic explanation linking TMEM127 to tumorigenesis.

Both support the internalization defect findings (C50-C54, C57). OpenEval emphasizes the biotinylation assay methodology and appropriate normalization, while peer reviewers accept this as 'compelling evidence' on reduced RET internalization without challenge.

Both support the broader claims about membrane organization and endocytosis defects (C4, C5, C6). OpenEval evaluates the synthesis of multiple experimental approaches, while peer reviewers affirm the 'convincing evidence' for inhibited endocytosis of multiple receptors.

Both support the RET-clathrin colocalization findings (C60-C65). OpenEval emphasizes the TIRFM methodology and appropriate normalization for increased RET, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the mechanism showing altered clathrin assembly.

Both support findings on reduced TIRF intensity (C66). OpenEval highlights the careful consideration of technical artifacts using complementary epifluorescence microscopy, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the clathrin distribution story.

Both support the CCP size and distribution findings (C70-C74). OpenEval emphasizes the super-resolution diSIM imaging and quantification of >6500 CCPs, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the mechanistic explanation for altered clathrin assembly.

Both support the CCP dynamics findings (C88-C93). OpenEval highlights the automated, unbiased detection methods, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the detailed characterization of how TMEM127 regulates membrane dynamics and clathrin distribution.

Both support the global membrane protein accumulation findings (C78-C81, C151-C152). OpenEval emphasizes the importance of demonstrating effects beyond RET, while peer reviewers explicitly praise this as a strength showing effects on multiple protein classes.

Both support the altered membrane dynamics findings (C97-C99, C157). OpenEval emphasizes the single-particle tracking methodology providing direct evidence, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the membrane dynamics story showing disorganization of lipid domains.

Both support the lipid microdomain findings (C115-C118). OpenEval notes this extends the phenotype beyond protein-protein interactions to lipid organization, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm the 'convincing evidence' for disorganization of plasma membrane lipid domains.

Both support the degradation findings (C120-C123). OpenEval emphasizes the appropriate cycloheximide chase experimental design, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the 'compelling evidence' on reduced RET degradation.

Both support the RET-dependent signaling and therapeutic implications (C130, C132, C138-C139, C141-C142, C154-C155). OpenEval highlights the use of multiple selective inhibitors, while peer reviewers accept the therapeutic implications and mechanistic link to tumorigenesis.

OpenEval supports the proliferation findings (C135-C137) as well-supported with appropriate replication. However, peer reviewers express uncertainty about the 'ligand-independent' interpretation, suggesting the mechanism may be more related to RET expression level/clustering rather than truly ligand-independent.

Both support the proximity ligation assay findings (C101-C105). OpenEval emphasizes the PLA approach is well-suited for detecting protein-protein interactions in situ, while peer reviewers describe the biochemical analysis as 'thorough and impressive.'

Both support the adaptor-clathrin interaction findings (C106-C114). OpenEval emphasizes the conclusion that interactions are intact but ineffective is important for the model, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the mechanistic explanation.

Both support the novel paradigm claims (C9, C10). OpenEval evaluates the synthesis as justified by convergent evidence, while peer reviewers view this as a significant contribution providing 'novel mechanisms and key insights' to cancer biology.

Both support the mechanistic model synthesis (C162-C163). OpenEval finds the model well-supported by multiple experimental observations and consistent with literature, while peer reviewers accept the findings as providing key insights to the field.

Both support the therapeutic implications (C166-C167). OpenEval notes the in vitro findings provide strong support for therapeutic rationale despite C167 relying on preliminary data, while peer reviewers accept the therapeutic potential as a strength with appropriate immunohistochemical support.

Both support the TMEM127 localization findings (C32-C36). OpenEval emphasizes the quantified, statistically significant immunofluorescence data, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the overall mechanism without challenge.
Both support the differential colocalization findings (C37-C39). OpenEval notes the appropriate use of GDNF stimulation, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the overall trafficking story.

Both support the mRNA-protein paradox findings (C43-C46). OpenEval notes the speculation about feedback regulation is appropriately cautious, while peer reviewers accept this as supporting the post-transcriptional mechanism.

Both support the generalizability findings in HEK293 cells (C48-C49). OpenEval emphasizes this demonstrates the phenotype is not cell-type specific, while peer reviewers accept this as supporting the global effect on membrane proteins.

Both support the recycling findings (C55-C56). OpenEval notes this rules out recycling as the primary defect, while peer reviewers accept this as supporting the conclusion that internalization is the primary defect.

Both support the membrane mobility findings (C95-C96). OpenEval emphasizes the single-particle tracking methodology, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the detailed membrane dynamics characterization.

OpenEval supports the ubiquitination machinery claims (C164) as appropriately citing preliminary data. However, peer reviewers express uncertainty, with Reviewer 1 specifically requesting discussion of how the clathrin-mediated and ubiquitin-mediated mechanisms relate to each other.

OpenEval rates predictions about other cancer types (C168-C173) as uncertain, noting they require experimental validation beyond PCC. Peer reviewers also express uncertainty, requesting more discussion on why TMEM127 loss is more linked to PCC and why it has broad effects on membrane molecules.

Both support the context-dependent TMEM127 function claims (C175-C178). OpenEval notes these appropriately cite supporting literature from other biological contexts, while peer reviewers accept these as important context and suggest discussing dual effects in tumor immunity.

Both support the Discussion summary claims (C147-C155). OpenEval finds the synthesis well-supported by presented data, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the overall 'convincing evidence' and mechanistic explanation.

Both support the global membrane protein accumulation summary (C151-C152). OpenEval evaluates this as appropriate recap of findings, while peer reviewers explicitly praise this as showing effects on multiple protein classes.

Both support the mechanistic model claims about membrane dynamics (C156). OpenEval finds this well-supported by TIRFM data, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the altered clathrin assembly mechanism.

Both support the CCP formation model claims (C158-C159). OpenEval finds this supported by live-cell CCP dynamics, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the mechanistic explanation for clathrin distribution effects.
Both support the membrane mobility interpretation (C157). OpenEval finds this supported by single-particle tracking, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the membrane dynamics story.

Both address the broader cancer implications (C172). OpenEval rates this as uncertain requiring validation in other cancer contexts, while peer reviewers support the paradigm as providing novel insights but request more discussion on cell type specificity.

Both address context-dependent functions (C181). OpenEval supports this as well-reasoned synthesis citing literature, while peer reviewers accept this and suggest discussing dual effects in tumor immunity contexts.
